canon.narrative.summary: Pepys rose at five and went to Chelsea, where the Lord Privy Seal passed his Tangier Privy Seal at first reading, and he was very joyed. This put him into a cruel melancholy, and he consulted with Creed about what to do. He also met Mr. Warren, from whom he feared his hopes would fail, and he went to bed with a headache, expecting to see the worst in a day or two.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys attended a Tangier Committee where Lord Ashley proposed that Povy remain Treasurer until his accounts were done; Pepys deflected the discussion but was troubled all day and night. Later he gave the Lord Treasurer, the Chancellor and the Duke of Albemarle an account of the Navy's charge and want of money, and they could offer only despair and no answer. He went home vexed, found women merry at Lady Batten's, was thrown on the bed in play, and was as merry as he could be despite being vexed before going to bed.
parsed.narrative.meaning: He finds it among the saddest things that, at such a critical time, nothing is minded and things are left to go on by themselves.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys goes early to Mr. Povy, wanting to settle his trouble of mind over the Tangier business, and offers to return the treasurership to him; Povy refuses. Creed then makes him doubt this, and Pepys gets Lord Barkeley and the Commissioners to order Povy's payment of his remaining accounts to him, to stop the matter being fastened on him. He spends the day dining with Creed, at White Hall, and with his wife at Mile-End Green, then goes home to bed. That morning he heard news that the fleets were engaged and Captain Teddiman had lost his legs, but by night he learns that this was false and that the fleet is well, and he is heartily glad.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys spends a busy day at the office and at Lord Treasurer's, then writes letters late at night, troubled that Sir W. Batten and Sir J. Minnes have noticed his absences and that he neglected a letter to Mr. Coventry, falling asleep and blotting it. The next day he makes up his monthly accounts, finds himself worth over £1400, and feels great joy. He receives Mr. Spong, admires his modesty and ingenuity, then goes to Woolwich and Deptford. He ends the month content with his estate but troubled about the Tangier business, and fearful of the sickness in the City.

raw_text: {"narrative.harm":"fear of the plague","narrative.summary":"The diarist woke and talked with his wife about a letter; she said she did not know its source, and he let the matter pass and they were friends. He spent the day on office business with Lord Bruncker, looking into the shipwrights' desertion over lack of pay, and they hoped the men would return the next day. He ended his letters at the office, then went home where W. Pen stayed to supper and they were merry together before bed.

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys works at the office, dines merrily with Sir W. Batten at Coll. Cleggat's, and is besieged by destitute prisoners and recovered sick men, to whom he gives good words and a little money. Luellin presses him to accept Mr. Deering's 20 gold pieces, which he takes against his will. That evening he sails to Woolwich and finds his wife upset over a quarrel with her maids, and he leaves angrily with suspicions about Mary and Brown. He returns, decides to smooth things over, sleeps contented, and ends the month with great content, praising God despite the plague.

After a pleasant afternoon he went to the office to write letters, then home with his head full of business and troubled that he had let his accounts go so far. He swore an oath that night to abstain from wine until he had passed his accounts. At home he shared a supper of little birds with the boy's sister, Mrs. Daniel, and kissed her, and earlier in the day he had also kissed Mrs. Burrows, who had called on him.

salience.tether.referent: oath to stop drinking wine until accounts are cleared
salience.tether.stake: unsettled accounts

parsed.narrative.summary: Pepys went aboard the Prince and agreed a £5,000 bargain with Sir Roger Cuttance for Lord Sandwich, nearly signing for the whole sum but escaping it by chance. Cleggat's, and is troubled by recovered sick men and prisoners left lying at the office doors with no provision. Luellin presses him to take Mr. Deering's 20 pieces in gold, which he accepts against his will. That evening at Woolwich he finds his wife out of order over a quarrel with her maids, and Mary's hint of something that would stop her mouth leaves him jealous and out of temper. He decides to smooth the matter over, goes to bed pleasantly, and ends the month with great content despite the plague.

He goes home by water through ice, a little frightened, and spends the evening at cards with Mrs. Tooker and the Daniels. Mr. Pierce then tells him W.
